<hypothesis>
To differentiate between the top candidate mechanisms (M11, M14, M16, M20), we need to exploit their different mathematical dependencies on substrate concentration during the deactivation step. 
- M14 deactivates via `catS => inactive`. Its deactivation rate will saturate once [S] is high enough to convert most of the catalyst into `catS`.
- M16 deactivates via `S + catS => inactive`. Its deactivation rate will continue to increase linearly with [S] even after the catalyst is fully saturated into `catS`.
- M11 deactivates via `S + cat => inactive`. At very high [S], free `cat` is depleted (shifted to `catS`), which creates a competing effect on the deactivation rate.
- M20 deactivates via both `cat` and `catS` spontaneously.

By running an experiment with the maximum allowable substrate concentration (S=5.0) and a low catalyst concentration (cat=0.01), we maximize the [S] to [cat] ratio. This will strongly amplify the deactivation rate in M16 (due to the high [S] multiplier on the saturated `catS` complex) while M14's deactivation rate will simply cap out. The low catalyst concentration ensures the reaction proceeds slowly enough for us to capture the full curvature of the deactivation profile before the substrate is depleted.
</hypothesis>
